text: Thank you. Thank you, Chief. Okay, we'll get right into it. And if you want to jump in and ask me about each of them, you're more than welcome to. So first of all, that 4.96 increase accounted for advanced hiring for confirmed retirements in the following year. And there was a total of five FTE. Last year, we had the possibility of eight members retiring. This year, we have the possibility of six. So we asked the board, I asked the board to allow us to get those folks to Ontario Police College and get them trained up for retirements that had put their letters in and so that we could have them on the street by the time that individual retired. The second point is a special compliment, special constable compliment was increased by two part-time FTEs. That was specifically related to our cell area and making sure that our prisoners that were suffering long-term drug addiction and mental health crisis had eyes and ears on them while they're in our custody, as opposed to a frontline police officer. And the third bullet point speaks to the issue of increasing our part-time staff compliment in the emergency operations center and data entry area by three part-time FTEs. If you go to the next slide, as most agencies that are in emergency services are feeling right now is the cost of vehicles, the lack of availability of vehicles and our vehicle leases increased year over year by 52 and a half percent, that's 377,000. And these costs of vehicles were increased due to the COVID and the lack of availability. When we were unable to buy the vehicles that we wanted to buy, we had to buy other vehicles that were higher grades. And just if you're wondering how long we keep our vehicles, a number of years ago, we used to keep them for three years and we found that in that third year, the vehicle costs went through the roof. Police vehicles for everyone have to understand they run 24, seven, 365 days a year. So basically they're only turned off when you're going through a shift change or they're getting an oil change. So vehicles are simply an ongoing cost and the lack of availability pushes up to 52 and a half percent increase. As part of that, we had to purchase a new K9 F-150 for our new K9 patrol. The current K9 member will be retiring soon. So we had to bring in new assets to replace that on the front line. Legal fees, as you can see in the third bullet point, increased by 25,000 or 32 or 33%. And that was to manage internal absences, requiring greater legal assistance when we bring people off of sick leave back into the office. And it's simply a protective preventative issue so that we make sure we follow the rules and don't end up in litigation. Computer increased 85,000. Many of you may not be aware, but the Sioux Police Service suffered a cyber attack back in September. And as a result of that, we had to spend obviously to get our data management system and our computer aided dispatch and our RMS niche system up to speed, as well as working with the provincial government to make sure that we were safe for the future to go forward. The photo equipment piece is 6,000 to replace out of date broken cameras and surveillance. That's an adequacy requirement that we have the most up-to-date equipment. And finally, the other capital increase of 218,000 included the NG911 or 80,000. It increased from 21. And that is for all the emergency radios in the Sioux area, all EMS work out of that NG911 cost. The last piece here is 210,000 for the building, including upgrades and repairs. We've had several health and safety complaints as recommended by the joint health and safety committee in conjunction with the ministry of labor. For example, the parking lot was deemed unsafe in terms of pedestrian walking into work. The HVAC system is constantly being repaired. Air quality, heating and cooling issues are a constant in the building and obviously have to be maintained. Next slide, please. So after we passed the budget, the ratification of the collective agreement came through. And basically what you're seeing there is there's 5.2% increase to the original 4.96. And that is basically where we are paying for three years of collective increase, collective agreement, FT increases. So you have two years of past wages that were negotiated. And then obviously for the 20 to 22 budget, you have a total of three years that you're paying for all at once. And that primarily accounts for, as you can see in the first bullet point, 6.14% of the increase. As a result of that collective agreement negotiation, there was an increase in retiree benefits. It was negotiated of 23.6%. WSIB chargebacks increased. We don't have any control over that. That's WSIB saying we need 10% more and insurance increases we have no control over. So there's the breakdown of your budget. Open to discussion.

So our five-year average of the DSAP has been a 1.34% increase. Unfortunately, this year, we are not in a position to be able to provide that to our municipal levy partners. And I'm going to get into some of the reasons for that very soon. Next slide, please. So when we rolled over our services from 2021 to 2022, without making any significant service reductions, we were presented with an 8.19% global net municipal levy increase year over year. A large percentage of that, 3.81%, was regarding our social service delivery, Ontario Works, housing, and early years. A large percentage of that resulted in EMS. In 2021, we had to add another 24-hour, 24-7-hour EMS truck to the road. We had a consultant do an organizational review and a projection in 2018. And that service enhancement was projected to be made at the 2021 budget year. When we looked at our call volumes, beginning of 2021, they were only up around 1.3%. So we recommended to the board that that decision be delayed until 2022. However, our paramedic services increased, our call volume increased an unprecedented call for service demand. In 2021, or 2020, sorry, we were averaging around 15,300 calls for service. We are projecting that by the end of 2021, that will exceed 17,000 calls for service. So it's an increase of over 10% year over year, which has been unprecedented for our service. Next slide, please. We went to the board with a global 8.19% in October, and we advised them that we had some recommendations on how to decrease our levy impact. One of the significant drivers on our social services side, Ontario Works Housing Services in early years, in 2019, 2020, the board began to make some strategic investments, and we began to look at entering into the full market tenancy apartments across the community. And we've purchased approximately 140 different units that are full market rents. And the strategy behind that was if we purchased full market rents and generated some type of operating surplus, that surplus could be then applied to reducing the levy. In 2022, all of our revenue will be online over the investments that the board has made strategically over the last year and a half. And it's resulted in a 300, in just over $300,000 decrease in our Sault Ste. Marie Housing Corporation operating budget, which is unprecedented as well. So the levy impact would have been much, much worse had the board not began to make that strategic shift in 2019, 2020. So as a result of the reduction in services that we recommended to the board, our social services impact is 0.13. Our land ambulance is an 18.12% increase in services. And then we also had a revenue decrease of $125,000. Interest rates are, as everyone who follows the market, are not what they were before the pandemic. As a result, some of our strategic investments and our reserve capital funds that we have at the DSEP are just not generating the interest return, the rate of return that they once did. And we use that interest rate, have we historically used that interest rate return to offset our levy increase. So as a result of the recommendation that the board, that we made to the board and they accepted, we are presenting the 3.11% budget increase to the board. Some of the reductions in services that that represented from the 8.19 down to 3.13. Ontario Works, we are transitioning out of being an employment-based service provider into a life stabilization service provider. And that transition is supposed to be complete by 2023, 2024 as per the Ministry of Community and Social Services. As a result, we felt comfortable recommending that the board decreased its employment related budget by $250,000 as we start to wind that division down. We also recommended to the board that we reduce, eliminate our investing in change fund, which is a $304,000 budget item. However, that budget item that we've taken out of 2022, we recommended to the board it could be removed because we are in an emergency response mode versus a strategic response mode. However, that investing in change fund was responsible for the establishment of Harvest Algoma. It was also responsible for the establishment of our low-income home ownership program. And if the board had not invested in Harvest Algoma, for example, 2019, our ability to weather the pandemic would have been severely, severely negatively impacted. So although we can recommend that that fund be removed from budget this year, we do see the value in driving innovation across the social services sector year over year. We also reduced our earlier budget by $108,000. There's a cost-share agreement with the province of Ontario that's been deferred throughout the pandemic. And so we held the line on our 2022 budget as to where we weren't, our 2021 line. We're optimistic that that could be a permanent reprieve. However, AMO and NAWZA and other groups have been lobbying the government hard to make sure that that cost-sharing arrangement is no longer there. But at this time, it's still on the books for a 2023 return, but we could eliminate it for this year. The other thing that we did throughout our EMS budget to reduce the levy impact, we had an ambulance because we did add another truck to the service. We also had to increase our capital acquisition. So we had added a new ambulance to the fleet. That is a cost of approximately $250,000. Rather than put that into levy, we recommended to the board that we use capital reserves to pay for that as it was a one-time cost and not a core operational cost, which the board accepted. The additional cost reduction in EMS result regarding an EMS base, we have been missing some of our response times throughout the central to downtown west area of the community. And we had planned on putting a new base online in 2022. However, just with the delays because of COVID and some of the construction materials, et cetera, we don't think that we're going to realistically get that base online until the end of 2022. So we took the rent and the mortgage payments out of budget completely and stated that we could cover up through operating for 2022. However, they will be making their way back in for the 2023 budget cycle. Next slide, please. One important thing to note to council and to the community, had we not had the significant surge in EMS call volumes in 2021, we would have presented the board with a 0.32% budget increase, levy increase. So the most significant portion of the 3.11 is in relation to EMS. And it is a service that is received and provided to the whole of the community. It needed to be added into the budget mid-year, but it is being felt throughout the 2022 budget year. Of other significant, just on the mitigation factors, 22% of our EMS calls in 2021 resulted in a non-patient transfer. Meaning 22% of the 17,000 calls that we went to, we responded lights and sirens. And when we got to the patient, the patient refused transport for one reason or another. A significant percentage of those non-urgent, of those non-patient transfers we're finding are in the elderly and the mental health and addictions lens. And we're very pleased to advise that the province of Ontario has provided the DSAB after many, many years of lobbying with a community paramedic service that will allow us to hire an additional seven FTEs into compliment after 100% municipal or provincial levy. We anticipate being able to strategically deploy some community paramedics where they can check on seniors, they can check on some people with known drug use and do some preemptive intervention prior to an emergency response being called. And we're hoping that we can start to bend the curve over the 2022 service, 2023 service years. So our budget was essentially zero. However, the addition to ambulance was a significant cost driver and that's the reason for the increase that we're highlighting to the community tonight. I believe that's the end of my presentation.

speaker: peterjohnson
text: Good evening. It's my pleasure to present to Mayor Provenzano and City Council of Fire Services 2022 budget. I'd like to thank the members of Sault Ste. Marie and Senior Fire Management Team for their commitment to the organization and the budget process. Deputy Chief Stuart Cole, Deputy Chief Paul Milosevic, Assistant Chief Dan Crozier, Office Supervisor Lisa McMillan. I also want to extend my appreciation to all staff at the Fire Service for their commitment to serve our community. The Sault Ste. Marie Fire Service is an external service that provides 24-hour, seven-day-a-week emergency response to the community. Fire Services consists of five divisions, administration, operations, where the primary objective is to provide emergency response to our community, fire prevention and public education, following the Ontario Fire Code and the provincial mandate from the Ontario Fire Marshal, the three lines of defense, which are public education, fire safety enforcement, and emergency response. Emergency management, where this role coordinates and develops the city's emergency plan. And support services, who's responsible for apparatus, fleet, equipment, building maintenance and repairs. Total staff compliment for Fire Service is 95. There are 89 union staff and six non-union staff. Next slide, please. Fire Services is presenting a 1.86% increase to the 2022 budget. Senior fire management has worked diligently within our budget to accomplish the goals and objectives to provide a sustainable, cost-efficient and effective fire service to the City of Sault Ste. Marie. Our major revenue is from our fire protection agreement with Batchewana and our open air burn permits. In the benefits portion, increases are related to Canada Pension Plan, OMERS contributions and WSIB, which includes presumptive cancer claims and occupational injuries. In other expenses, the 4.2% increase is directly related to our operating expenses for the service. These increases will be explained in a few slides. Also included is a 2% cost of business inflationary increase as detailed by finance last Monday. Next slide, please. Key initiatives from 2021 and looking ahead to 2022 include through council resolution and subsequent approval, Fire Services Cost Recovery By-law, which includes responses to false alarms, natural gas leaks without locates has been recognized to recover over $17,000. The third party cost recovery for insured perils will commence in 2022. This could see potential of up to $50,000 in recoveries. Open air permits have been a major source of revenue for fire services for a number of years. In 2020, during COVID, 2,300 permits were processed. To date in 2021, our revenue for these permits is slightly over $110,000. The same value is projected for 2022. With council approval, Sault Ste. Marie is a designated regional training center with the Ontario Fire College. We've been recently approved to host several courses in 2022. Major benefit for this designation is staff will have less or limited travel to achieve our training goals and objectives. And we will be able to host quality programs and courses to the region. Next slide, please. The following items represent the 4.21% increase in other expenses for fire services. These are contained in the preliminary budget as presented. First increase located on the agenda under travel and training is $25,000. This is to operate and fund our post-traumatic stress disorder program, which is called peer support. This important program requires a new professional service provider and agreement that will enhance, train and support staff. The previous provider's agreement is no longer current. This program is supported by legislative bill 163, the Supporting Ontario's First Responder Act, 2016. The goal of the peer support program is to mitigate or prevent PTSD for staff and reduce potential costs associated with claims. The second increase on the same page is for $10,000 for medical and personal protective equipment for medical responses. The funds will be utilized for items such as N95s and surgical masks, face shields, medical gloves and medical equipment. During COVID, costs associated with required medical supplies has increased. Further response protocols have changed as well as protective equipment required to be worn. These industry changes will be the accepted practices for medical responses. Prior to EMS transferring to DSAB, our supplies were restocked by EMS. This is no longer happening as they are no longer a city department. The third increase on the same page is for $8,080. $6,000 for that increase is related to advanced inspections of bunker gear and the remaining $2,080 is directly related to the 2% inflationary increase. Fire services staff require their bunker gear, which is structural firefighting gear, to be advanced inspected and tested. This enhances our existing program and ensures staff are wearing gear that has been inspected and meets NFPA 1851 standard. Previously, this was done every three years. The standard was recently revised and now requires annual testing. This includes a complete liner inspection, which includes hydrostatic testing of the barrier and a visual inspection of the inner surface of the thermal liner. The total number of sets to be tested will be approximately 200 sets. The final increase of $6,121 represents the applied 2% inflationary increase. The $312,151 is transferred from our operating budget to our capital reserves to assist in funding future capital purchases.

speaker: mayonprovenzano
text: Next slide, please.

speaker: peterjohnson
text: Fire services has four capital requests for 2022. The first request includes upgrading the radio communication system to a digital system. This request addresses our communications for all personnel. This is a health and safety concern as the current system is analog. We have multiple areas in the community where dead spots affect our radio transmissions. Due to the age of the current system, we have experienced some items that have been difficult to service. Firefighters depend on their radios as a lifeline when conducting interior operations to receive and relay information to and from command. Other areas of major concern, the system is not encrypted. Therefore, the general public that have access to a scanner can hear all of our radio communications. This has been a concern and in further discussion with police services whose system is encrypted, we have had incidents where we support each other, but our communications are public. This will eliminate any potential for confidential information to be shared while communicating via radio transmissions. Equally, the addresses, locations and nature of the incident will not be heard over a scanner. Annually, fire services spends about $5,000 towards repairs, replacement of radios and the system. A new system would eliminate or reduce this amount. Risks associated with not approving, fire services would continue to use the current system, experience difficulties in communications and not have an encrypted radio system. There would be continued exposure to confidential information being transmitted. Next slide, please. The second capital request is for $130,000 to replace four daily fleet vehicles. Fire services utilizes a number of apparatus, vehicles and equipment to provide efficient and effective service to the community. As part of our asset management plan, there is a replacement schedule to follow when replacing these vehicles. Our support services division has been able to extend the life expectancy of our fleet vehicles. They are now beyond their life expectancy and value versus the cost of repair. Examples of the mechanical issues are engine exhaust manifolds, brakes, tires, catalytic converters, leaking head gaskets, corrosion and extensive body repairs to the vehicles. These vehicles are critical to the daily function of our service delivery for fire prevention. Risks associated with not approving, staff would not have vehicles to perform their roles. This would create inefficiencies and backlogs in our process for our service to the community. We would also see an increase in our vehicle maintenance and repair costs. The third capital request is for $65,000 to replace our frontline response platoon chief vehicle. As per the ministry of labor field visits during fire services realignment, we were instructed to revise our operating guidelines to reflect the current staff model. A platoon chief vehicle is an integral response unit to meet the minimum on scene staff to make entry to perform interior fire operations. There must be seven on scene in order to make entry. This revision was approved by the ministry. This current vehicle is a 2011 and is at the end of its lifespan for frontline response. It has been included in our fleet replacement schedule and it's not unforeseen requests, it has been forecast. The fourth request is to replace a 2004 one-ton utility truck for $65,000. This unit is used to pull the airboat hazmat trailer and our on scene rehab trailer for firefighters. It also serves as a backup to the platoon chief vehicle when out of service. Replacing our apparatus and fleet vehicles adhere to the approved fire master plan recommendation number 42, which states fire service sustain its current fleet and major apparatus at all times. Next slide, please. Fire services submitted a supplemental request to the operating budget to increase the amount of funds transferred from our operating budget to our fire capital reserves for apparatus, vehicles and equipment. As highlighted last Monday by CFO Schell, the request provides options for council's consideration to plan for future capital purchases. Currently we transfer 312,151 annually to fund those capital purchases. Fire capital reserve is currently underfunded to meet the financial requirements to purchase mandatory vehicles to meet the approved level of service. The consequences of not funding these purchases will result in an older fleet, which could result in issues for part sourcing for repairs, increase in mechanical failure, which could affect responses and increases to maintenance and repairs. If not funded through the capital reserves, debt financing would have to be considered to make future purchases. And that concludes fire services presentation. Thank you.
